Discussion has 38 of the 75 minutes, and the deck 3 more. The two
problems and the simulation have 30, feedback included.

**If the room is slow.** Give each activity's feedback at its time
even if some groups have not finished: the Solution box is the
feedback. Take time from discussion 3 first (it can be folded into
the simulation's feedback), then from the close. Keep discussions 2, 4
and 5. The two problems are longer than the two they replaced on 19
October. If short, take (a) to (c) of problem 1 and give (d) in its
feedback, and (a) and (c) of problem 2 and give (b) in its feedback.

The exercises at the top of the sheet (1 to 13; 11 to 13 in R) are
for students' own time and outside the 80 minutes. Say so. No marks
are attached to any of them. The three prompts and "Three claims"
under "If there is time" are reserves. (Until 19 October the class's
problems were the false rejections and group membership and $R^2$; the
convenor's convention of that day, exercises before problems with the
class working the problems, made them exercises 1 and 2 and made the
old problems 12 and 11 the class's problems 1 and 2.)

## Feedback, hints and solutions

The complete sheet is the one on the screen. Each of the three
in-class activities is followed at once by its feedback: open the
Solution box and go through it, three or four minutes each. There is
no separate block of solutions later.

The hints for problems 1 and 2 are in the complete sheet and not in
the student sheet: open them in order when a group has been stuck for
a few minutes. The simulation has no hint, because its starter code
runs as given. The hints for the exercises are in the student
sheet. Solutions are in the complete sheet only and are not released
afterward.

## Discussion 1: the two studies of infants

The two studies were set as reading and are not in the lecture, so
this is the only place they are discussed. Five minutes in groups,
four with the room. The prompt is "How convincing is the study's main
claim?" and the sheet has no subquestions.

- There is no house answer. Take one reason for "convincing" and one
  for "not convincing" from each study and leave it there. The course
  makes no claim about whether either result has held up, and neither
  should the class.
- Follow-up questions, if a group is stuck: What is the main claim?
  (The abstract states it.) How many infants? Which
  comparisons does the abstract report, and which do the same tables
  allow that the paper does not report?
- The facts are in the box "The two papers" under the prompt and in
  the notes' section "Two studies of infants," which has the tables as
  charts. Put that section on the screen for the last two minutes.
- In each paper some of the comparisons the data allow reached the
  abstract and a figure, and others got a sentence of text or nothing.
  Stop short of saying the authors chose what to report after seeing
  the results. The papers do not show that.
- If a student compares the text of Alexander and colleagues with its
  Figure 1 and finds they disagree about the boys: they do. The
  journal published an erratum in 2010 correcting the sentence; the
  notes have it.
- If a student has looked up whether either study has been replicated,
  let them report what they found as their own finding, with its
  source, and move on.

## What the class works that the lecture only stated

The lecture has three parts and a five-minute close, planned at 75
minutes with 5 of slack: mindless statistics (34 minutes: cargo-cult
statistics, the null ritual, six statements about a $p$-value),
groups and individuals (17 minutes), and the variance argument with
the largest of $n$ (19 minutes). The class takes two of its arguments to cases the lecture
did not work, simulates a third result, and spends the rest of its
time in discussion.

- **The recall question.** In the lecture's simulation the slope was
  the same for people and for area averages, and $R^2$ rose from
  $0.20$ to $0.84$ (population values; $0.19$ and $0.85$ in the
  simulated draw on the slide). "In the lecture's simulation model"
  is part of the question, because the answer depends on the model.
  When each area has an effect of its own, $R^2$ still rises but no
  longer tends to 1 (exercise 6). When everyone else's rate varies
  with the group's share, as in exercise 5, the slope across areas is
  not the difference between the two groups' rates. The derivation
  for the lecture's model is exercise 4; problem 1 takes the same
  question to a newspaper's table.
- **Problem 1.** A newspaper's table of the 32 London boroughs, with a
  correlation of 0.6 across boroughs read as a fact about how graduates
  vote: what the table identifies (a relationship between borough
  rates), why a share of adults and a share of votes cast are not
  shares of the same people (turnout), the constancy assumption under
  which ecological regression gives graduates' support, and what the
  Duncan--Davis bounds would add. Ecological regression, constancy and
  the bounds are not in the lecture; the notes have them, and the stem
  of (c) says how the regression is read. Exercises 5, 7 and 9 work the
  same ideas with numbers. It was optional problem 12 until 19 October.
- **Problem 2.** The tail arithmetic of the lecture's variance
  argument, with constants that can be used by hand: a standard
  deviation 10% larger gives about 1.5 times the rate above two of
  group 1's standard deviations, and 60% of the prize-winners. (b)
  sorts Hyde and Mertz's (2009) numbers into averages, spreads and
  tails, and (c) is the lecture's slide "Assumptions at each step" as a
  question. It ends at the step from two distributions to one
  applicant, where discussion 2 starts. It was optional problem 11
  until 19 October.
- **The simulation.** The lecture gave the largest of $n$ four
  minutes: the probability that the larger group's item is the more
  extreme, $0.99$ for 100 items against 10,000, and one slide of
  formulas. Those three slides are the last thing in the lecture's cut
  order, so ask whether they were shown; the notes have the same
  example under "The largest of $n$." Students run the starter code,
  then predict and check $0.75$ for 1,000 against 3,000.
- **Exercises.** 1 is last week's formula for the share of rejections
  that are false, which the lecture recalled after the room marked six
  statements about $p = 0.01$ (all six false): $0.009/0.059 = 0.15$
  (notes: "The null ritual"). 2 derives $d^2/(d^2 + 4)$ by the law of
  total variance, from the lecture's slide on statistical
  discrimination ($d = 0.5$, 6% of the variance); its part (b), that a
  chart of two group means has an $R^2$ of 1, links to the recall
  question. Until 19 October these two were the class's problems 1 and
  2. 3 is the misread $p$-value. 4 is aggregation and $R^2$, the
  derivation behind the recall question. 5 is ecological regression on
  two areas: area rates $0.29$ and $0.34$, line $0.265 + 0.25x$, so the
  regression reports $0.515$ for a group whose rate is $0.2$, because
  everyone else's rate rises with the group's share. It was problem 2
  until the convenor swapped it out on 6 October, as too close to
  substitution into a formula. 6 and 7 continue 4 and 5. Two slopes
  (8) and the bounds (9) are not in the lecture; the notes have both.
  10 is the largest of $n$ by hand. 11 to 13 are in R: 11 builds the
  people-and-areas plot, 12 is the largest of $n$, 13 is ecological
  regression on fifty precincts. "Three claims," under "If there is
  time," sorts three claims from the week by averages, spreads and
  tails, and by people and places.

## Expected misconceptions

In class:

1. **"Averaging biases the slope."** It does not, under the lecture's
   simulation model: both regressions estimate $\beta$. What averaging
   changes is $R^2$, through the variance (exercise 4(b) asks for that
   word).
2. **"The ecological correlation is just wrong."** Robinson's
   correlation across the 48 states, $0.53$ between foreign birth and
   literacy as Freedman (1999) gives it ($-0.526$ with illiteracy in
   Robinson 1950, p. 354), is a correct correlation between states. It answers a question about
   states. The error is reading it as an answer about people. Problem 1(a)
   is the same point about boroughs.
3. **"The line is wrong," and "more areas would fix it."** In problem 1(c),
   as in exercise 5, the line is a correct summary of the area rates. The error is reading its two ends
   as the two groups' rates. That error is a bias, from the constancy
   assumption, and is a different thing from what averaging does to
   $R^2$. Under a failing constancy assumption the estimate converges
   to the wrong number: exercise 7(a) shows that the fitted slope contains
   $\gamma$ however many areas there are. A related one: "the area
   data would show if constancy failed." Sometimes they do (a curved
   scatter, a fitted rate above 1), but a straight scatter does not
   confirm it.
4. **"A small group's bounds are always 0 to 1."** That was
   Washington. In exercise 9(a) a group of the same size has bounds of
   0 to 0.125, because the outcome is rarer than the group. The rule,
   which problem 1(d) needs, is in exercise 9(b).
5. **Tails read as averages.** In problem 2 and in "Three claims," "boys are better at
   math" is a claim about averages and the number quoted (a
   99th-percentile ratio) is about tails. Make them say which of the
   three (average, spread, tail) each number is about. This is the
   week's sensitive topic; the lecture notes open with the convenor's
   statement that the reading of the examples is his and that
   disagreement is not penalized. Keep it on the arithmetic (which
   number, which group, who took the test) and on Hyde and Mertz's
   Table 2. The variance ratio differs between countries, which
   challenges a universal ratio and does not by itself exclude an
   intrinsic contribution; why it differs is a causal question, for
   next week.
6. **"So group averages tell you nothing."** The overcorrection. A
   group average is a fact about the group; exercise 2 says how much of
   a member it describes, and the bounds (exercise 9) say what area
   data settle. Discussion 2 is the place for it.
7. **"The larger group is more extreme," and "every time."** In the
   simulation the two groups have the same distribution. Students who
   conclude the 10,000-post group is "worse" have made the inference
   the week is about. And the larger group's post is the more extreme
   with probability 0.99, not 1; about two reversals in 200 days are
   expected, and none at all in about one run in seven.
8. **The two skimmed studies, as a verdict.** Students will want to
   say whether Connellan et al. or Alexander et al. "replicated." The
   course makes no claim either way and neither should the class.
9. **"No significant difference" read as "no difference."** Alexander
   and colleagues' looking-time analysis did not find a statistically
   significant sex difference; the means in the text still differ.
   Last week's material: a test that does not reject is not evidence
   of equality.

In the exercises, if students raise them:

10. **1% or 99% in exercise 1.** They will want the level or its
    complement. The answer needs the share of real effects and the
    power: 15% here. If someone says the chance of a wrong rejection is
    the level, the level is $P(\text{reject} \mid H_0)$ and the exercise
    asks for $P(H_0 \mid \text{reject})$.
11. **$d^2$ for $d^2/4$ in exercise 2(a).** They take the distance
    between the two group means as each mean's distance from the middle.
    Each mean is $d/2$ from the mean of everyone, so the variance
    between groups is $(d/2)^2$. With $d = 1$ the slip gives a share of
    $1/2$ where the answer is $1/5$.
12. **"The two bars differ, so the groups differ."** Exercise 2(b). Two
    means always fit a line perfectly. With $d = 0.2$, 99% of the
    variation is inside the groups.
13. **$0.56$ for $0.59$ in exercise 4(a).** They have used 1 for the variance of
    the area averages. It is $1 + 4/n$: the average of $n$ people still
    contains a little of the within-area variation. At $n = 400$ the
    two agree to two decimals; at $n = 1$ their formula gives 0.05
    where the answer must be 0.20, which is the quick way to show them.

## Discussion prompts

The sheet gives one question for each discussion and no subquestions.
The examples and follow-up questions below are for the teacher, to use
if a group is stuck. None of the five has a house answer.

- **Discussion 2: "When is it reasonable to use information about
  someone's group to make a decision about them?"** It follows problem
  2, where membership of a group accounted for 1% of the variance at
  $d = 0.2$ and 20% at $d = 1$, and it is close to the question the
  lecture put to pairs
  ("Is an aggregate claim about a group ever a claim about a member of
  it?"). The plot on the screen has the area averages in a line and
  the people in a cloud. Cases, if the room needs one: an insurer
  pricing one driver from the claims of drivers of the same age; a
  doctor quoting a five-year survival rate to one patient; an employer
  screening applicants by the average of their school. Things that
  differ between them, as possible follow-ups: whether better
  information about the person could be had, and at what cost; whether
  the person chose to be in the group; whether the decision is made
  for the person or about them; who pays when the group's rate is
  wrong for them; whether the group's average is itself the result of
  past exclusion (the lecture's slide "Decisions from group
  averages").
- **Discussion 3: "A feed shows the most extreme post from each group.
  How should readers interpret what they see?"** It follows the
  simulation's feedback. Arguments the room may make: the shown post
  says little about a typical post from either group, since both shown
  posts were far from typical when the groups were identical; the
  difference between the two shown posts can come from the number of
  posts alone; a reader usually does not know how many posts each
  group made, or what the feed ranks on. Possible follow-ups: What
  would you want to know before concluding anything about a group from
  its most extreme post? Does it change anything if the groups do
  differ in spread (exercise 10(c)(iii))? Whose job is it, the
  reader's or the feed's? Rathje and colleagues, in the optional
  reading, found that posts about the political out-group were shared
  or retweeted about twice as often as posts about the in-group
  (Rathje and colleagues 2021), so the people who share select before a feed
  ranks anything.
- **Discussion 4: "A junior analyst disagrees with the conclusion
  their manager wants to publish. What should they do?"** The scenario
  is bare on purpose. Let groups ask what the disagreement is about
  and say how their answer depends on it. Possible follow-ups: Is it
  an error, or a choice that could reasonably have gone either way
  (which comparison to report, which model)? Who is affected if the
  conclusion is wrong? What can the analyst do short of refusing: ask
  for the assumption to be stated, for a range, for the other analysis
  to be reported beside it? What does each option cost them? From the
  week, if wanted: Stark and Saltelli's "We can stand up for the
  responsible use of statistics, even when that means taking personal
  risks" (a lecture slide); Feynman's wish for the graduating class,
  "the good luck to be somewhere where you are free to maintain the
  kind of integrity I have described" (the notes); and the lens "You
  have to choose, so choose, and defend it." A group may equally argue
  that a choice which could reasonably go either way is the manager's
  to make, provided it is stated.
- **Discussion 5: "Could AI make cargo-cult statistics worse, or help
  solve the problem?"** The convenor shows a separate in-class deck
  first, with material from Luo, Kasirzadeh and Shah, "The More You
  Automate, the Less You See: Hidden Pitfalls of AI Scientist Systems"
  (2025, <https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08713>). The deck is not part of
  this packet, and the prompt stands without it. From the paper's
  abstract: it identifies four potential failure modes in AI scientist
  systems (inappropriate benchmark selection, data leakage, metric
  misuse, and post-hoc selection bias), finds several of them in two
  open-source systems, and reports that they are detected far more
  effectively from trace logs and code than from the final paper
  alone. About three minutes for the deck, then groups, then the room.
  Arguments the room may make. Worse: Stark and Saltelli wrote, "The more 'powerful' and
  'user-friendly' the software is, the more it invites cargo-cult
  statistics," and the notes ask what they would
  say about software that writes the analysis for you; post-hoc
  selection is week 1's selection, run automatically. Help: a complete
  log of what was run is the record Feynman asks for ("Details that
  could throw doubt on your interpretation must be given, if you know
  them"), and a tool can check an assumption that an analyst in a
  hurry skips. Possible follow-up: who checks the output, and what
  would they need to see?

### If there is time

- **A good critic.** From the 2024 class. No house answer.
- **What was selected.** Each group takes one setting. The prompt does
  not presume that the selection misleads or that anyone gains from
  it; "it does not matter here" is an answer a group can defend.
  Possible arguments:
  - Most-improved boroughs: the table selects on a large change in a
    measure that is partly noise. If so, the selected boroughs will on
    average improve less the following year, and some will fall back
    (regression to the mean, week 1's schools prompt at area level).
    That is a statement about the average of the selected boroughs,
    not about any one of them, and it depends on how much of a year's
    change is noise.
  - Top-ten posts from one side: the largest ten of a number of posts
    the reader does not see; the simulation again.
  - The crime map: an ecological correlation that a reader may take as
    a fact about people; the constancy assumption is the unstated
    step. The one to handle carefully. Keep it on the arithmetic (what
    would the bounds say?) and off the demographic variable.
  - Top picks: selection on a score the user does not see, from a pool
    of unknown size. A group may argue that this selection is what the
    user wants.
  - Best fund managers: the largest of $n$ noisy returns (week 1's
    winner's curse). A group may argue that some of the ranking is
    skill; how much is the question.
- **Two models, one number.** Freedman's Table 2 is in the notes, not
  the lecture. These aggregate data alone do not establish which model
  is correct. Answers a group can defend include a range (the two
  estimates, or the bounds of exercise 9), a qualified
  estimate with its assumption stated, and a recommendation to get
  data on individuals before publishing a number. The notes' table
  also shows the survey's answer, 28%; the prompt leaves it out
  because an analyst in this position would not have it. It is
  outside the range between the two estimates, and inside the bounds,
  which contain the truth by construction.

## Notation

In exercise 5 and the exercises that continue it, areas are
indexed by $i$, as in Freedman: $p_i$ is the rate in the group of
interest and $q_i$ the rate among everyone else; $x_i$ is the group's
share of area $i$, $y_i$ the area's rate; problem 1 uses the same
letters without the index, with graduates as the group. In exercises 4
and 6,
$X_{ij} = B_j + W_{ij}$ for person $i$ in area $j$: $B_j$ is shared by
everyone in the area (variance $\sigma_B^2$), $W_{ij}$ is the person's
deviation (mean zero, variance $\sigma_W^2$, uncorrelated with $B_j$
and across people). $d$ in exercise 2 is the difference between two
group means in within-group standard deviations; $G$ in its Solution
is the group. In exercise 8, $b_B$,
$b_W$ and $b_{\text{all}}$ are the slope across area averages, the
pooled slope within areas and the slope across everyone, and $\lambda$
is the between-area share of the variance of $X$. $M_n$ is the largest
of $n$ draws. The two groups in problem 2 are "group 1" and "group
2." Register 1 throughout; the symbols $A$, $R$ and $U$ are not used
this week (the area effect in exercise 6 is a lowercase $u_j$).
